claims.text: The as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a uniform, nonequilibrium metastable solid solution.
The initial alloy contains no detectable intermetallic compounds.
Nonequilibrium manufacturing processes can produce chemical short-range-order states that differ from equilibrium states.
The particular Mg-containing alloy initially possesses nonequilibrium chemical short-range order.
Thermal exposure causes the initial nonequilibrium short-range order to relax or reorder.
Short-range-order relaxation provides a driving force for selective Mg segregation.
Selective Mg segregation produces diffusion-limited nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Moderate thermal aging produces a fine dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates can nucleate a continuous protective Mg-oxide scale.
Formation of the continuous protective oxide scale maintains or improves corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Formation of the continuous protective oxide scale maintains or improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
More aggressive high-temperature or prolonged exposure accelerates intermetallic growth and coarsening.
Aggressive exposure produces coarsened or network-like intermetallic compounds.
Coarsened intermetallic networks disrupt oxide-scale continuity and integrity.
Disruption of oxide-scale integrity causes a measurable loss of corrosion resistance.
Disruption of oxide-scale integrity causes a measurable loss of high-temperature oxidation resistance.
At temperatures above approximately 500°C, diffusion is sufficiently rapid to promote intermetallic phase formation in the alloy.
Below approximately 500°C, the metastable solid-solution state may be largely retained.
Comparable oxide scales, corrosion behavior, and intermetallic distributions after moderate and aggressive aging would falsify the proposed mediation by intermetallic evolution.
